answers.asked: "There's no real point to predefining a 'transition point'. For a Gamma sweep just plot amplitude as a function of gamma going up and down."
answers.answer: Done that way. No transition point is defined or computed anywhere tonight; each sweep is one figure of pattern amplitude against Gamma with the way up and the way down marked and the steps not yet done shown as ticks under the axis. The figures are in evidence/fastpass-figures/: one per frequency for the no-friction model (ten, redrawn from whatever each loop has finished), and one for the nudge at f* 0.44 from the finished pilot. Only one figure has both branches so far, f* 0.44 without friction across the onset (the pilot left running on November 15, which finished): flat layer amplitude 0.025 of a particle diameter; on the way up it is still 0.10 at Gamma 2.2 and reaches 0.43 at 2.4 and 0.56 at 2.7; on the way down it is still 0.34 at 2.2, 0.14 at 2.1, and flat again by 1.95. So at 25 cycles per step the two branches are apart between about Gamma 2.05 and 2.4, by up to 0.24 of a diameter. That is one seed at the fast rate and is what a pattern that needs time to grow would also give.
answers.departures: The figures are SVG files drawn directly, because the program's environment has no plotting library. Each branch is drawn twice: solid for the amplitude with the uniform (shot-noise) part of the spectrum removed, dashed for the raw amplitude in the pattern's wavelength band; that choice of amplitude was not in the instruction (decision D0039).

answers.asked: "Pick configurations (3d only). Pick frequencies (say 10). At the fast rate go up and down in gamma. Look at the amplitude plots. Near transition go back and go up and down much slower to look for hysteresis just at those points."
answers.answer: Started, not finished. Configuration: the paper's three-dimensional layer (60000 spheres, depth 5.42). Ten frequencies: f* 0.27, 0.30, 0.33, 0.38, 0.44, 0.50, 0.57, 0.65, 0.74, 0.84. Fast rate: Gamma 1.7 up to 7.0 and back in steps of 0.05, 25 cycles a step, one seed (213 steps a loop). How far it got: 684 of 2130 steps of the no-friction pass (f* 0.84: 124 of 213 steps, at Gamma 6.15 on the way down, largest amplitude so far 0.67; f* 0.74: 109 of 213 steps, at Gamma 6.9 on the way down, largest amplitude so far 1.06; f* 0.65: 93 of 213 steps, at Gamma 6.3 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.11; f* 0.57: 84 of 213 steps, at Gamma 5.85 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.08; f* 0.50: 76 of 213 steps, at Gamma 5.45 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 0.90; f* 0.44: 98 of 213 steps, at Gamma 6.55 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.04; f* 0.38: 59 of 213 steps, at Gamma 4.6 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.04; f* 0.33: 41 of 213 steps, at Gamma 3.7 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.49; f* 0.30: queued; f* 0.27: queued). 2 of the ten have reached Gamma 7.0 and turned round (f* 0.84, 0.74) but none is back down to the onset, so apart from the pilot at f* 0.44 there is still no way down across an onset to compare with. What the way up shows so far: at f* 0.33, 0.38 and 0.44 a strong pattern from the first onset (amplitude about 1.4, 1.0 and 0.6 of a diameter, rising near Gamma 1.95, 2.1 and 2.3). At f* 0.50 to 0.84 the first pattern is weak (at most 0.09 to 0.15 of a diameter, between Gamma 2.2 and 3.0) and fades to nothing measurable by Gamma 3.0 to 4.0; then the amplitude rises a second time, sharply, to 0.65 to 1.1 of a diameter, starting near Gamma 4.1 at f* 0.50, 4.2 at 0.57, 4.5 at 0.65, 4.9 at 0.74 and 5.3 at 0.84. At f* 0.44 the same second rise shows as a step up near Gamma 4.5 with a longer wavelength. I have not looked at the fields themselves, so I am not naming these patterns. What remains: the rest of these ten loops (about 115 CPU-hours; the eight running should finish during the day of November 17, the two slowest about a day later), then the other two models. Slow loops: none started, as instructed. Where I would put them, from the plots so far, each at 100 cycles per step (four times slower) first and 400 only where the gap survives: at the first onset, where the pattern is strong: f* 0.33, Gamma 1.75 to 2.25 and back (on the way up the amplitude goes from 0.00 at 1.8 to 0.78 at 2.0); f* 0.38, Gamma 1.85 to 2.4 (0.06 at 2.0, 0.77 at 2.2); f* 0.44, Gamma 1.9 to 2.6 (0.10 at 2.2, 0.43 at 2.4; the one place with both branches). At the second rise, which is the sharper one at the higher frequencies: f* 0.50, Gamma 3.9 to 4.5 (0.00 at 4.0, 0.32 at 4.2); f* 0.57, Gamma 3.9 to 4.7 (0.06 at 4.0, 0.43 at 4.4); f* 0.65, Gamma 4.3 to 4.9 (0.04 at 4.4, 0.47 at 4.6); f* 0.74, Gamma 4.6 to 5.2 (0.21 at 4.8, 0.51 at 5.0); f* 0.84, Gamma 5.0 to 5.6 (0.10 at 5.2, 0.34 at 5.4); f* 0.44, Gamma 4.2 to 4.8 (0.43 at 4.2, 0.66 at 4.6). The fast loops at f* 0.84 and 0.74 are on their way down and will cross their second rise within hours, which will show whether there is anything to slow down for there. At f* 0.44 that slow loop is priced at 8 CPU-hours at 100 cycles per step and 32 at 400; at other frequencies scale by 0.44/f* and allow half as much again.
answers.departures: The f* 0.44 loop reuses the finished pilot's first 21 steps (Gamma 1.7 to 2.7) instead of recomputing them. Each loop keeps its saved states only at Gamma multiples of 0.5, to stay inside the disk budget. Each loop stops itself at 38 CPU-hours so none can pass the 40 CPU-hour per-run limit unasked. My prices were too low: I priced the ten no-friction loops at 80 CPU-hours and the steps done so far put them at about 154 (ten jobs share the machine, so somewhat high).

answers.asked: "Do that all for the different models."
answers.answer: Not yet: only the no-friction model is running. Nudge: no loop run tonight. Its price per loop is 16 to 35 CPU-hours for f* 0.84 down to 0.38, and 40, 44 and 49 for f* 0.33, 0.30 and 0.27, which are at or over the 40 CPU-hour per-run limit, so those three are reported and not started. I queued the two cheapest nudge loops behind the no-friction ones and then withdrew them before either started, when the no-friction loops looked, in their first hour, to cost 1.4 to 1.7 times their price, which would have taken the week to about 89 percent on their own. With more steps in, the no-friction pass prices at about 154 CPU-hours and takes the week to about 80 percent, so there is room for one or two nudge loops this week, not ten. Where the nudge stops and why, from the pilot at f* 0.44: going down from Gamma 3.0 its cost climbs from 15 to 55 CPU-seconds per cycle at 2.25 and it does not finish 25 cycles at 2.2 inside half a CPU-hour; its pattern is gone (amplitude 0.04 or less) from Gamma 2.4 down, so it does reach the flat layer, just, but it cannot be held there or started there at a sensible cost. Its loop is therefore planned as: start at 3.0, down to that floor, up to 7.0, back down. Baseline (friction, no contact method): no loop run and none priced; in three dimensions it needs an upward push to start at Gamma 3 and has stopped below Gamma 2.3 to 2.8 and at Gamma 5 in earlier runs, so its loops will be short branches.
answers.departures: Withdrawing the two queued nudge loops was my decision (D0041), made to keep an unattended queue from taking the weekly budget to its limit.

answers.asked: "Gamma: whole range, let's see what it can do."
answers.answer: The loops are set to the whole range, 1.7 to 7.0 and back, and are on their way up. The furthest is f* 0.44 without friction, at Gamma 6.55. So far the no-friction engine has done every step asked of it: 684 steps finished, 0 with a slow stretch, 0 cycles failing the energy audit, 0 steps that did not complete. What it can do above Gamma 6.55 is not known yet.

answers.asked: "Configurations: let's start there [the paper's layer], but our plan should be to add depths: the hysteresis should be more obvious in deeper layers."
answers.answer: Tonight ran only the paper's layer. The plan now adds depths next (evidence/phase-diagram-plan.md, section 0b), with cost. Twice the depth (10.84, 120000 spheres) costs about 3.8 times as much per loop; three times the depth about 15 times, which puts every full loop over the per-run limit. The pattern's wavelength grows with depth, so at twice the depth the 100-wide box holds 3.9 wavelengths at f* 0.84, 2.8 at 0.57, 2.2 at 0.44 and 1.3 at 0.27: the low frequencies need a wider box, at four times the cost again. Proposed: one short run at twice the depth to measure the cost (0.2 CPU-hours); then no-friction loops across the onset only (Gamma 1.7 to 3.0 and back) at f* 0.84, 0.74, 0.65 and 0.57, about 37 CPU-hours for the four; the full range and the lower frequencies only where those show the branches apart. These factors are scaled from two-dimensional costs, not measured in three dimensions.

answers.asked: "Add the no-friction freezing test to tonight's instruction." "2D is fine for the freezing test. That said, I am mostly just curious whether we get freezing in that case; it's not really that valuable."
answers.answer: Yes, we get freezing with friction off, but only a little and only when the rest threshold is raised a hundredfold. Whether it acted: at the current threshold (1e-4) one sphere went to rest once in twelve runs, and eleven of the twelve runs are bit-for-bit the no-friction baseline, so they test nothing. At 1e-3 there were 134 rests in 4 of 12 runs. At 1e-2 there were 124741 rests in 9 of 12 runs, and at 3e-2, 180250 in 10 of 12. Frozen against phase: resting spheres appear only in the last quarter of the cycle and the first sixteenth of the next, while the plate is pushing up; never more than one sphere at depth 5. The most spheres frozen at any recorded instant was 5 of 1500 at 1e-2 and 17 of 1500 at 3e-2; the largest frozen region was 3 and 6 spheres. Nearly every rest is ended by the next hit within a fraction of a cycle (97 and 94 percent of them); 40 and 219 lasted until the plate let go. Energy audit: no failing cycle in any of the 48 runs. Bulk quantities against the no-friction baseline: all pass at 1e-4 and 1e-3 (mostly identical runs), 11 of 11 completed runs pass at 1e-2, 6 of 7 at 3e-2. Raising the threshold breaks runs the unmodified engine completes: 1 of 12 failed at 1e-2 and 5 of 12 at 3e-2 (three with the resting-pair solver giving up, one overlap, one at its CPU limit). Per condition and threshold: evidence/E0062-results.json. No follow-up started.
answers.departures: Four thresholds: 1e-4 (current), 1e-3, 1e-2, 3e-2. At 3e-2 the wake threshold was raised to 3e-2 as well, because the design needs it at or above the rest threshold, so that column changes two settings. The build is the region-freezing branch at its tip (the Nov 11 design plus the energy-bookkeeping fix), pinned with friction off as method/persistent-contact-mu0. Frozen counts are sampled 32 times a cycle, so most of the brief rests are in the totals but not in the per-phase counts.

answers.asked: "What holds up a ball is multiple contacts that balance the force on the ball. So really, our freezing ideas are bad because we are trying to freeze something in an unphysical way... in 2d i can see an approach where instead of freezing at one contact, we can freeze when velocities are low and ball B is scheduled to hit both A and C within some delta. In 3D I guess there is also a ball D? This also should help with the balls on the plate where balls on the side are what constrain the central ball." Asked whether the agent should check the existing stalls against this criterion tonight: "Yes, add it."
answers.answer: Checked, at the seven stalls examined on November 12 (first stall of the engine with friction at each stalled two-dimensional condition). Would the criterion have fired: on the sphere on the plate, yes at 6 of the 6 stalls that are a pressed pair, at any delta, but only if a touching contact counts as 'scheduled' and 'low velocity' means the closing speed at the contacts; and the two contacts it fires on are the plate and the pressing sphere, which do not balance the push (0 of 6). A third contact that does balance it is within 0.001 of a diameter at 1 of 6 stalls, within 0.01 at 4 of 6, within 0.1 at 6 of 6; that neighbour is due to hit in 0.003, 0.05, 0.10 and 0.18 time units (0.0002 to 0.023 of a drive period) at closing speeds of 0.016 to 0.06, and at 2 of 6 stalls no side neighbour is approaching at all. So a three-contact version would need a delta of about 0.2 time units and a speed limit near 0.06, and at that delta 10 to 19 percent of the whole layer has three partners due. On the pressing sphere: no; it touches only the sphere below it at all 6, its next partner is due in 0.03 to 0.41 time units or never, and it is moving at 0.10 to 1.29. Velocities are the catch: the closing speeds at the stalled contacts are 1e-11 to 1e-10, but the spheres themselves are not slow (the lower one rolls at 0.03 to 0.65 relative to the plate). The seventh stall is different and fits the criterion cleanly: one sphere held on the plate by two spheres above it, 30 degrees either side, all three contacts touching, speed 0.0002. Neighbour counts by gap, positions and due times for every stall: evidence/E0063-results.json.
answers.departures: The instruction said no new engine runs. The November 12 replays saved only the stalling pair, not the layer around it, so I reran those seven replays (the same deterministic runs to the same stall, checked equal in cycle, phase and spheres; 28 CPU-seconds in all) and then only read the state. Two readings were mine: a partner closer than 1e-9 of a diameter counts as due now (taken literally, a contact that has just bounced has no next collision on a free flight, and then the criterion fires on the lower sphere at only 3 of 7 stalls); and 'balance' is tested with normal forces only, in the plane. Only the first stall of each condition at seed 1 was examined, not the four persistent-contact stalls of November 11, which are the same conditions with a different engine.

headline: Tonight started the fast pass you asked for: ten no-friction Gamma loops in the paper's three-dimensional layer, drawn as amplitude against Gamma with no transition point; 684 of 2130 steps are done, the eight running loops are past Gamma 3.6 and two have turned round at 7.0; they need another day or so.  The freezing build with friction off does freeze, but only a handful of spheres for moments at a time and only with the threshold raised a hundredfold; and at the examined stalls the two-contact criterion would fire on the sphere on the plate but on contacts that do not balance it, while the balancing side neighbour is usually a few hundredths of a diameter away.

experiments.question: Left running on November 15: in the full three-dimensional box without friction, what does the amplitude read in a flat layer, and what does a loop across the onset cost?
experiments.what_was_done: Collected. The loop (60000 spheres, f* 0.44, Gamma 1.7 up to 2.7 and back in steps of 0.05, 25 cycles a step) finished on the morning of November 16 once the lid was opened.
experiments.result: All 41 steps completed with no slow stretch and no energy-audit failure, for 3.1 CPU-hours. The flat layer reads 0.025 of a particle diameter and the striped layer at Gamma 2.7 reads 0.56. The cost falls from 21 CPU-seconds per cycle at Gamma 1.7 to 7 at 2.7.
experiments.takeaway: All four things I predicted held. It is the first loop of the fast pass and the only one with both branches so far: they are apart between Gamma 2.05 and 2.4. One seed at the fast rate, so not a result about hysteresis.

experiments.question: Left running on November 15: what does the nudge cost below Gamma 2.5 in the full three-dimensional box, and where does it stop?
experiments.what_was_done: Collected. From the nudge's striped state at Gamma 3.0, f* 0.44, Gamma was stepped down by 0.05 every 25 cycles with half a CPU-hour allowed per step.
experiments.result: It completed every step down to Gamma 2.25 and ran out of its allowance at 2.2. Cost per cycle: 15 CPU-seconds at Gamma 3.0, 25 at 2.5, 36 at 2.3, 55 at 2.25. The pattern's amplitude falls from 0.42 of a diameter at 3.0 to 0.04 or less from 2.4 down. No energy-audit failure. 3.1 CPU-hours.
experiments.takeaway: All three predictions held. At this frequency the nudge does reach a layer with no pattern before it becomes too slow, with a margin of about 0.15 in Gamma. The floor is set by the half-hour allowance; a larger one moves it.

experiments.question: The fast pass, no-friction model: what does the pattern amplitude do as Gamma is stepped from 1.7 up to 7.0 and back at each of ten frequencies?
experiments.what_was_done: Ten loops in the paper's layer (60000 spheres), one seed, steps of 0.05 in Gamma, 25 cycles a step, eight running at a time since 23:11 with the two slowest queued behind them. The height field is recorded at every step and its amplitude drawn against Gamma, one figure per frequency.
experiments.result: Not finished: 684 of 2130 steps, 36.9 CPU-hours tonight. F* 0.84: 124 of 213 steps, at Gamma 6.15 on the way down, largest amplitude so far 0.67; f* 0.74: 109 of 213 steps, at Gamma 6.9 on the way down, largest amplitude so far 1.06; f* 0.65: 93 of 213 steps, at Gamma 6.3 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.11; f* 0.57: 84 of 213 steps, at Gamma 5.85 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.08; f* 0.50: 76 of 213 steps, at Gamma 5.45 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 0.90; f* 0.44: 98 of 213 steps, at Gamma 6.55 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.04; f* 0.38: 59 of 213 steps, at Gamma 4.6 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.04; f* 0.33: 41 of 213 steps, at Gamma 3.7 on the way up, largest amplitude so far 1.49; f* 0.30: queued; f* 0.27: queued. No step has had a slow stretch, failed the energy audit or failed to complete. On the way up the pattern is strong from the first onset at f* 0.33 to 0.44 (amplitude 0.6 to 1.4 of a diameter); at f* 0.50 to 0.84 the first pattern is weak (at most 0.09 to 0.15) and fades by Gamma 3.0 to 4.0, and a second, sharp rise to 0.65 to 1.1 of a diameter follows between Gamma 4.1 and 5.4, later at higher frequency. The loops cost more than I priced: above Gamma 2.7 the f* 0.44 loop takes about 8.6 CPU-seconds per cycle where I had assumed 4.
experiments.takeaway: Too early to say anything about hysteresis: no loop is back down across its onset. The engine is doing what was asked of it. The pass will cost about 154 CPU-hours rather than 80. It will be judged against what I registered when it ends; so far every step has completed and every running loop has shown an amplitude above 0.2 of a diameter. The sharp second rises at the higher frequencies are the most promising places to look for hysteresis once the loops come back down through them. The loops are left running.

experiments.question: The fast pass, nudge model.
experiments.what_was_done: Priced, and the two cheapest loops (f* 0.84 and 0.74) queued behind the no-friction loops; then withdrawn before either started.
experiments.result: Nothing was run. Prices per loop run from 16 CPU-hours at f* 0.84 to 49 at f* 0.27, about 300 for the ten; the three lowest frequencies are at or over the per-run limit.
experiments.takeaway: Recorded as abandoned. The no-friction pass takes the week's CPU budget to about 80 percent, so a ten-frequency nudge pass needs either more budget, fewer frequencies or later weeks. That is a question for you below.

experiments.question: With friction switched off, does the region-freezing build (spheres rest on the plate and on resting spheres) freeze anything, and what does it do to the layer?
experiments.what_was_done: 48 two-dimensional runs: the twelve conditions of the referee's grid, one seed, 120 cycles, at four rest thresholds from the current one (1e-4) up to 3e-2, after a two-run pilot. At every recorded instant (32 per cycle) I counted the resting spheres and the largest connected group of them, and compared the usual bulk quantities with the no-friction runs of the unmodified engine. Two cores, 1.1 CPU-hours.
experiments.result: At the current threshold freezing does not act: one rest in twelve runs, eleven runs identical to the baseline. Rests number 134 at 1e-3, 124741 at 1e-2 and 180250 at 3e-2, but they last moments: at most 5 spheres of 1500 are resting at any recorded instant at 1e-2 and 17 at 3e-2 (1.1 percent), in groups of at most 3 and 6, always while the plate pushes upward. No energy-audit failure anywhere. Every completed run but one passes the bulk comparison; the exception, at 3e-2, is off in all seven quantities by five to nine standard deviations. One run in twelve fails at 1e-2 and five in twelve at 3e-2, at conditions the unmodified engine completes.
experiments.takeaway: I predicted that a raised threshold would freeze more than a tenth of the layer; it froze about a hundredth at most, so that prediction failed. Without friction there is very little for this rule to freeze, and pushing the threshold up to make it act mostly makes runs fail. This fits your point that a sphere held by one supporter is not really at rest: almost every rest is undone by the next hit. No follow-up, as instructed. One slip in my ledger note for this test: it says 97 to 98 percent of rests end at the next hit; the counts given there are right and make it 97 and 94 percent.

experiments.question: At the stalls already examined, would 'freeze when velocities are low and the ball is due to hit two others within some delta' have fired, and at what delta?
experiments.what_was_done: For the seven stalls of November 12 I recovered the whole layer at the stall and, for the sphere on the plate and the sphere pressed on it, listed every neighbour within a tenth of a diameter: its gap, its direction, its closing speed and when it is next due to collide. I then asked whether the contacts within each gap could balance the push on the sphere, and applied the same criterion to every sphere in the layer as a control.
experiments.result: Six stalls are a sphere on the plate with one sphere pressed on it at 22 to 61 degrees from vertical. In all six the lower sphere touches exactly two things, the plate and the pressing sphere, and those cannot balance the sideways push. The nearest neighbour that could is 0.0002 to 0.03 of a diameter away; it closes the balance within a gap of 0.001 at one stall, 0.01 at four, 0.1 at all six, and is due to arrive in 0.003 to 0.18 time units at four stalls and not approaching at two. The upper sphere touches only the lower one and is moving at 0.1 to 1.3. The seventh stall is one slow sphere held on the plate by two spheres above it, three touching contacts.
experiments.takeaway: Recorded as failed on one of my three predictions, on a technicality worth knowing: a contact that has just bounced is not 'scheduled' to hit again, so the criterion needs to count touching contacts, not only scheduled collisions. More important for the idea: at these stalls two contacts are always present but never balance, and the balancing third contact is close but not yet touching, arriving at speeds a few hundred times the rest thresholds tried so far. A criterion loose enough to include it would also catch a tenth or more of the layer. The one stall with three balanced touching contacts is the case the idea handles cleanly.

questions.question: The no-friction pass will take this week's CPU budget to about 80 percent of 400 CPU-hours, and the nudge pass is priced at about 300 more. Raise the limit, run the nudge (and baseline) at fewer frequencies, or let them wait for later weeks?
questions.why_it_matters: 'Do that all for the different models' cannot fit in one week at ten frequencies under the present limit, and the three lowest-frequency nudge loops are each at or over the 40 CPU-hour per-run limit.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Finish the ten no-friction loops. Then start nudge loops one at a time from the highest frequency down, only while the week's count stays under the limit, and start nothing priced over 40 CPU-hours.

questions.question: For a model with friction, is 'start at Gamma 3.0, go down until a step costs too much, up to 7.0, and back down' the loop you want, with 'too much' meaning half a CPU-hour for 25 cycles?
questions.why_it_matters: The nudge cannot start in the flat layer or stay in it cheaply, so its loop has no flat end to speak of; where it turns round is set by the cost allowance, not by physics.

questions.question: In your freezing criterion, should 'velocities are low' mean the closing speeds at the contacts, and should a ball already touching another count as 'scheduled to hit' it?
questions.why_it_matters: At the stalls the spheres themselves are not slow (the one on the plate rolls at up to 0.65) while the closing speeds are a hundred-billionth; and a contact that has just bounced has no scheduled collision. Read strictly on either point, the criterion does not fire on most of the stalls.
questions.default_if_unanswered: No design or build either way; freezing work stays paused. The check is recorded with both readings.

questions.question: Where do you want the first slow loops? My two candidates, both without friction at 100 cycles per step: f* 0.44, Gamma 1.9 to 2.6 and back (about 8 CPU-hours), where the pilot's branches are apart; and f* 0.65, Gamma 4.3 to 4.9 and back, where the way up jumps from 0.04 to 0.47 of a diameter in 0.2 of Gamma.
questions.why_it_matters: The first is the only place with both branches so far, and tells us quickly whether a gap at the fast rate closes when the ramp is four times slower. The second is the sharpest rise seen tonight; its way down is not in yet.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Start none; redraw the figures as the loops finish and list candidates again.

questions.question: For deeper layers: may I run one short hold at twice the depth to measure its cost (0.2 CPU-hours), and then loops across the onset only at the four highest frequencies (about 37 CPU-hours)?
questions.why_it_matters: A full ten-frequency pass at twice the depth is about 300 CPU-hours or more, and the low frequencies no longer fit three wavelengths in the box.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Run neither until the no-friction pass at the paper's depth is finished and you have seen it.

proposed_directions.direction: Let the ten no-friction loops finish, redraw the figures, and list where the two branches differ at each frequency.
proposed_directions.rationale: It is the pass you asked for and it is running; nothing about hysteresis can be said until the loops come back down.

proposed_directions.direction: Slow loops at f* 0.44 across Gamma 1.9 to 2.6, and across the sharpest second rise once its way down is in, four times slower.
proposed_directions.rationale: The cheapest direct test of whether the gap seen at the fast rate is ramp lag. It is yours to place; this is where I would put the first.

proposed_directions.direction: Nudge loops from the highest frequency down, as the budget allows.
proposed_directions.rationale: The second model. The high frequencies are the cheapest and are where the nudge's loop is most likely to run the whole range.

unfinished_runs.reason: ten no-friction loops, 684 of 2130 steps done; eight running, two queued behind them (runs/fastpass-1116b.spec); each step is saved, so a loop resumes from its last finished step

run_conditions.limits_hit: The machine was awake on AC power with the lid open all session: no sleep or wake events in the power log, so the lid problem of November 15 did not recur and that blocker is closed. Nothing else was running at the start (load average 1.8, so 12 of 14 cores free). What limited the science was wall clock and the core limit: ten cores for a pass that needs about 154 CPU-hours means the loops will not finish for another day or more, and tonight shows mostly their way up. Ten jobs at once also slow each other, so tonight's costs per cycle are upper estimates. For about a minute at 23:18 up to twelve simulations were running against the limit of ten, because I started the stall replays with the wrong queue setting; I stopped that queue and reran the rest inside the limit. CPU-hours are from the runs' own records: 36.9 for the loops (not counting 1.6 copied from the pilot), 1.1 for the freezing test and under 0.01 for the stall replays; the two pilots collected tonight used 6.2 between sessions. Budget: the ledger counts 167 CPU-hours this week and the loops in progress add 36.9, so the week stands at about 51 percent: past the 50 percent mark, and it will reach about 80 percent when the loops finish. Disk: 43 GB free at the end against a floor of 40, program data 5.1 of 15 GB; the loops will add about 2 GB more, which brings free disk close to the floor. Memory 61 percent free at the start; each loop uses about 0.2 GB.
